AGENDA
Part one

The production floor

Modules A, B and C of the Phase 2 proposal — supervisor entry, the operator station, and the records that flow out of them.

Part one · the change

The record now happens at the machine, not after the shift

How it works today
  • Cart records are written on paper at the line, then keyed into the Excel daily report afterwards.
  • A supervisor spends roughly two hours a day on that entry.
  • A cart that was run but never written down is simply gone — nothing can detect it later.
  • Efficiency per operator is calculated by hand, after the fact.
  • Half a cart carried into the next shift lives only in someone’s memory.
In the system
  • The operator enters the cart at the line, as it finishes — timestamped, tied to a badge and a machine.
  • Work order, tray count and material carry over; the operator confirms rather than re-types.
  • Half-cart carry-over is a required choice on the first cart of a shift, and is inherited downstream.
  • The supervisor sees who is logged in on which machine, live.
  • At sign-out the operator reviews the shift and signs, or disputes it.

OPERATOR STATION
Part one · one cart, one record

The whole shift is this one screen, repeated

  • 1

    Everything above the cart number is inherited

    The level-2 work order carries over from the last cart. The operator confirms it; typing it again is optional.

  • 2

    Half-cart carry-over is decided here

    The amber banner offers to continue the previous shift’s final cart. Dry room, reports and the Sage sync all inherit that link — it is never asked again.

  • 3

    Only two numbers are actually typed

    Tray count and output. The cart number advances by itself; the level-1 order is matched from a scan or a typed number.

  • 4

    One cart can carry several level-1 orders

    Each with its own quantity — which is what makes per-work-order material usage add up instead of blurring across orders.

/worker · Inj 01
MODULE B
Part one · supervisor

Shift Assignment: scan the line, scan the badge

  • 1

    One pair at a time

    Scan the machine, then the badge, then Confirm. Scan the line again to add a second person.

  • 2

    No scanner? Type into the same box

    Inj 01 or 1001 — spaces and case do not matter. The board still works when the scanner does not.

  • 3

    Logged in, not signed out

    Anyone who badged into a tablet appears here, assigned or not, and joins the roster with one tap. It never blocks an unassigned operator — it catches up with the floor rather than gating it.

  • 4

    The roster is a roster

    It records who was on which line — it does not split the line’s output between individuals.

Part one · supervisor

Line QR codes — the piece that has to exist in the plant

Production · Floor · Line QR codes
45
machines with a code ready to print — Inj 01–30, EXT 01/02 and the rest
1×
printed once, taped to the machine, then scanned every shift

The payload is LINE:<machine code>, generated by the same function the scanner reads. There is no second list to keep in step.

This is the one physical prerequisite. Until the codes are on the machines, the scan flow on the previous slide has nothing to scan and the supervisor falls back to typing.

What happens when the operator disagrees with the record

Production · Floor · Confirmation Disputes

At sign-out the tablet shows the operator their own shift — carts, trays, total output — and asks for a signature.

  • ✓

    Sign

    The shift closes and a confirmation sheet is archived.

  • !

    Dispute

    The shift stays open and lands on this page. The supervisor resolves it; the operator still has to sign afterwards.

Empty is the normal state — an exception queue, not a daily task. This is the live test system, with no dispute open.

The raw-material chain

Part two · the problem

Today the stock figure is wrong for as long as the order runs

MODULE F · PROBLEM
Part two · the change

Two ledgers, and the movement is posted when it happens

MODULE F · LEDGERS
Part two · how the quantity is decided

The quantity comes from the formula, not from experience

  • 1

    The formula is versioned

    Lines, quantities and a scrap allowance per SKU. A new version retires the old one; batches already mixed keep the version they used.

  • 2

    The work order carries a planned weight

    Entered when the order is opened. Run through the formula, it produces the requirement for every powder.

  • 3

    Mix room first, store room for the shortfall

    Whatever the mixing room already holds is used first; only the gap becomes a pick from the store room.

  • 4

    Lots are chosen by the system

    Oldest expiry first. Lot numbers and quantities land on the pick document, so nobody decides on the floor.

Requirement per powder
planned weight
  ÷ formula base output
  × line quantity
  × (1 + scrap %)
Tracked on every requirement line
  • Required — what the formula says the order needs
  • Issued — what the store room actually released, by lot
  • Consumed — what the mixer says actually went in
MODULE F · FORMULA
Part two · the link back to the cart

The pallet is what joins powder to product

MODULE F · TRACEABILITY
Part two · what it gives back

Plan against actual, per work order

What becomes answerable
  • How much of this powder is really available right now — store room and mixing room, separately, at any moment.
  • What this order actually cost in material — required, issued and consumed side by side, per powder.
  • Which orders run heavy — deviation against the formula, order after order, as a loss baseline.
  • Where a bad lot went — from the supplier lot forward to every cart it touched.
Rules that keep the numbers honest
  • A scale reading beats a bag count. Bags with a unit weight and an opened-bag weight are accepted, but weighing wins.
  • Powder borrowed from another product’s mix is allowed and recorded, not blocked — blocking it would stop the line and teach people to work around the system.
  • Stock cannot go negative, and an issue always names a lot.
  • The formula version is frozen onto the batch, so a formula change never rewrites history.

STATUS · PART TWO
What we need from NPIC

Four decisions only NPIC can make

01

Who owns the formulas, and where do the first ones come from?

Maintained by whom, approved by whom, loaded from Sage or typed in. Nothing in the mixing module runs until one formula exists.

02

When both ledgers together are short, does the system stop the order or flag it?

Blocking is cleaner on paper and stops the line in practice. This is a plant decision, not a software one.

03

Units, and the printed pick document

Which unit each powder is counted in, and what the store-room and mixing-room copies need to show to be usable as they are today.

04

The Sage 100 environment

Version, connection method, credentials, and the field mapping for orders, BOM, stock and lots. Integration is last in the schedule but the longest lead item — worth locking now.
